title: 道德經 第五十五章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 55, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 80. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 55 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 玄符 (The Dark Token). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
含德之厚，
比於赤子。
蜂蠆虺蛇不螫，
猛獸不據，
攫鳥不搏。

morph.gloss: to hold in, to keep within — properly to hold something in the mouth
potency — the power a thing has by simply being what it is
of (genitive) — it makes 含德 into a noun, 'the holding of potency'
thick, deep-laid — what has body to it
to be comparable to, to stand beside for comparison — with 於 bringing in what it is set beside
to (the all-purpose preposition, standing after its verb)
a newborn child — literally a 'red child', from the raw colour of the newly born
red, raw-red — of the newly born
a child, an infant
wasp, hornet
scorpion
an adder — a small venomous snake
snake
not
to sting — of a venomous creature
fierce, savage
a beast, a four-footed animal
not
to seize and pin down with the claws; to lay hold of
to snatch with the talons
a bird
not
to strike at, to grapple with, to seize

sentences.i: A man in whom potency is held thick is like a newborn child. Wasps and scorpions, adders and snakes do not sting him; wild beasts do not pounce on him; birds of prey do not strike.
sentences.n:
含德之厚 is four characters with no subject and no verb 'to be': 'the thickness of holding-potency-in'. 比於赤子 is the comment on that topic and not an order to the reader — there is no imperative here, only 'comparable to a newborn child'. 之 is the genitive doing what English needs a whole clause for, and Wang Bi supplies the missing person outright when he comments — 含德之厚者, 'the one who is thick in it'.

The newborn is this chapter's single image, and everything that follows is observation of an actual infant: the loose bones, the tight fist, the day-long crying. 赤子 'red child' is the ordinary word for a baby, not a coinage of the book's.

The three creature-clauses have no object at all — Chinese does not say who is not stung, seized or struck, and English has to put 'him' back in. The witnesses differ over which creatures are in the list and how many clauses it runs to; ours has three.

morph.gloss: bone, the bones
weak, soft — here the whole comment on 骨, with no verb between
sinew, tendon — what pulls the bones
supple, pliant — the yielding quality of the newborn and of water
and yet
a grip, a clenched fist — the verb 'to grasp' standing as a noun
firm, holding fast

sentences.l: Bones weak, sinews supple — and yet the grip firm.
sentences.i: His bones are weak and his sinews soft, and yet his fist holds fast.
sentences.n:
Two topic–comment pairs with nothing joining them: 骨弱 is 'bone — weak', and there is no verb to be had. Then 而 carries the entire turn of the argument, 'and yet'.

Anyone who has put a finger into a baby's hand knows the observation is exact, and it is the book's thesis in seven characters: soft is not the same as feeble. 柔 and 弱 will come back paired as the mark of the living.

morph.gloss: not yet — it leaves the thing still to come, where 不 simply denies it
to know
female and male — the two sexes of animals
the female of an animal, the dam that bears young
the male of an animal, the sire
of (genitive) — it makes a noun of the clause: 'the female-and-male's joining'
a joining, a coming together — the verb used as a noun
and yet
whole, entire, with nothing lost off it
to rise up, to stir into action; Wang Bi glosses it 長, 'to grow'

sentences.l: Not yet knowing the joining of female and male, and yet whole he stirs,
sentences.i: He has never known the union of female and male, and yet, entire in himself, he stirs;
sentences.n:
The chapter's one real crux, in four characters. Our text reads 全作, 'whole, he stirs', and Wang Bi's comment glosses 作 as 長 'to grow': nothing has drained the infant, so he is entire and grows. Some other editions, and the silk manuscripts from Mawangdui, read not 全 quán but 朘 zuī — the infant's member — which turns the line into a plain physiological observation: he has never known coupling, and yet it stiffens. That reading suits the run of the chapter, which is all body (the fist, the voice, the breath). We keep the text Wang Bi read and his gloss on it, as the sole-source rule requires, and leave the other reading here where you can weigh it.

未 is 'not yet', not 'not': it denies the thing so far and leaves it coming.

sentences.t:
精之至也。
終日號而不嗄，

morph.gloss: the finest essence — the concentrated vital stuff at the heart of a thing
of (genitive)
the utmost, the far point reached
final particle: closes the statement as settled, 'that is what it is'
right through, to the end of
the day
to howl, to cry out — read háo 'to wail', not hào 'a title'
and yet
not
to go hoarse, to lose the voice — a rare character, and the editions write it several ways

sentences.l:
The utmost of essence, that is what it is.
The day through he howls, and yet does not go hoarse —
sentences.i: That is essence at its height. He can cry the whole day and never grow hoarse —
sentences.n:
X 之至也 is this chapter's refrain — 'the utmost of X, that is what this is' — and it comes twice. Each time it passes judgement on the line before it, not the line after: it is a verdict, not a heading. 也 is not the modern Mandarin 'also' but a full stop with an air of finality.

精 is not 'spirit'. The word properly means hulled, cleaned grain — the concentrated best of a substance — and here the vital stuff itself, undissipated because nothing has yet spent it.

sentences.t:
和之至也。
知和曰常，

morph.gloss: accord, blending — things sounding together without one drowning another (read hé)
of (genitive)
the utmost
final particle, closing the statement
to know
accord
is called — it fastens a name onto what precedes
the abiding, what is always so

sentences.l:
The utmost of accord, that is what it is.
To know accord is called the abiding;
sentences.i: That is accord at its height. To know accord is what is called the abiding;
sentences.n:
曰 is the naming word: A 曰 B, 'A is called B'. It comes four times in the next four lines, each time fastening a name onto a state, and the four names are not all compliments.

和 is the sounding-together of chapter 2's 音聲相和. The infant who cries all day and does not go hoarse is in accord with himself: nothing in him is working against anything else, so nothing is spent.

Wang Bi glosses the line 物以和為常，故知和則得常也 — 'things take accord as what abides in them, so knowing accord is having hold of the abiding.' The line does not say 'to know what abides': that is the next line's business, and the two would collapse into one if it did.

morph.gloss: to know
the abiding
is called
clear sight, seeing clear

sentences.l: To know the abiding is called seeing clear.
sentences.n: This line is chapter 16's, word for word. The book quotes itself, and the repetition is deliberate rather than an editor's slip — there the clarity came of watching things return to their root, here of watching an infant.

morph.gloss: to add to, to increase
life, the living
is called
an omen, a portent — usually a lucky one, which is what gives the line its bite

sentences.l: To add to life is called an omen.
sentences.n:
祥 ordinarily means a good omen, and reading it that way here makes nonsense of the line — so it must be the neutral 'portent', with the context making it a bad one. Wang Bi is blunt about why: 生不可益，益之則夭也, 'life cannot be added to; add to it and it dies young'. What is meant is the whole regimen that tries to force life upward — nourishing, hoarding, prolonging — set against the infant, who does nothing to himself at all.

祥 xiáng and the 強 qiáng of the next line rhyme, and the rhyme has survived into Mandarin. Read the two lines together and you can hear that they are one verdict in two halves.

morph.gloss: the heart-mind — thinking and feeling in one organ; in this book the schemer
to make, to drive, to set to work (the plain causative)
breath, vital energy — the animating stuff of the body
is called
strength, the forceful — read qiáng 'strong', not qiǎng 'to compel'; in this book never praise

sentences.l: The heart-mind driving the breath is called strength.
sentences.i: For the heart-mind to drive the breath is called being strong.
sentences.n:
使 is the bare causative: 心 the subject, 使 the verb, 氣 the thing made to do something. In the infant the breath goes of itself; 強 is what you get when the mind takes the reins of it.

強 is one of this book's steady villains — chapter 30's 果而勿強, and the stiffness that belongs to what is dead — so 'strong' here is a diagnosis. Set beside the line before it: forcing life and forcing breath are one fault said twice.

sentences.t:
物壯則老，
謂之不道，
不道早已。

morph.gloss: a thing, a creature
at full strength, in its prime — the state just before decline
then, and so — it introduces the consequence
to grow old, to pass into age and decay
to call, to name
it — here the OBJECT pronoun, not the genitive
not
to go the Way — the noun used as a verb, which is why 不 can negate it
not
to go the Way
early, before its time
to stop, to be done — the full verb here, not the closing particle

sentences.l:
A creature at full vigour then grows old:
call it not-going-the-Way,
and not-going-the-Way comes early to its end.
sentences.i: A thing at its mightiest is already ageing: this is called not going by the Way, and what does not go by the Way is soon finished.
sentences.n:
These three clauses closed chapter 30 as well, with one character different: there 是謂 'this is called', here 謂之 'call it', with 之 as the object pronoun. Nothing turns on the difference, and the repetition tells you this was a saying the book could reach for twice.

老 lǎo and 道 dào rhyme, in Old Chinese and still in Mandarin — worth reading aloud.
